extracted.intended_audience: school administrators, Title IX coordinators, and institutional legal counsel (K-12 and postsecondary)
extracted.subtask_description: Standards and procedural requirements that educational institutions must follow when adopting, conducting, and publishing Title IX grievance procedures for sexual harassment/sexual misconduct complaints, including investigation, hearing, evidence, timelines, and protections. Emphasizes due-process considerations, live-hearing and cross-examination rules for postsecondary institutions, and related regulatory constraints.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fundamental/basic fairness and adherence to institution's own policies
rubrics_metrics.description: Private school disciplinary procedures must adhere to a 'fundamental' or 'basic' fairness standard and comport with the rules and procedures that the school itself has promulgated; decisions should not be arbitrary or capricious.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts often hold that private-school disciplinary decisions are fundamentally fair if they follow the institution's own published procedures (Lisa Tenerowicz; Kathryn M. Reardon; Holly Hogan). Even absent constitutional protections, institutions must comply with their own rules.

rubrics_metrics.name: Minimum procedural safeguards (Goss baseline)
rubrics_metrics.description: At minimum, disciplinary procedures should provide: (1) adequate notice of the charges; (2) reasonable opportunity to prepare for and meet them; (3) an orderly hearing adapted to the nature of the case; and (4) a fair and impartial decision.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Goss v. Lopez establishes these 'bare minimum' requirements. The disciplinarian, when apprised of disputes, may summon accuser, permit cross-examination, allow the student to present witnesses, and in difficult cases permit counsel. These measures reduce risk of erroneous action.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mathews balancing test to determine required due process
rubrics_metrics.description: The appropriate level of procedural protections is determined by balancing interests, per Mathews v. Eldridge, to decide when judicial-type procedures must be imposed on administrative action to assure fairness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Application is context-specific: weigh private interest, risk of erroneous deprivation, and government/institutional interest. Mathews is cited repeatedly as the governing test for how much process is constitutionally required.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinction: academic decision vs disciplinary misconduct
rubrics_metrics.description: Courts give greater deference to institutions' academic decisions and require more stringent procedural protections for dismissals based on disciplinary (non-academic) misconduct than for academic dismissals.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: See Bd. of Curators of Univ. of Mo. v. Horowitz: academic matters receive more deference; disciplinary decisions require more procedural safeguards when liberty/interests are at stake.

rubrics_metrics.name: Live-hearing requirement for postsecondary formal complaints (§106.45(b)(6)(i))
rubrics_metrics.description: Postsecondary institutions are required to use a live hearing model to adjudicate formal Title IX complaints.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The final regulations impose a live hearing model for postsecondary institutions. Elementary and secondary schools are not required by §106.45(b)(6)(ii) to hold any kind of hearing to adjudicate formal complaints.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cross-examination must be conducted by an advisor (no direct party questioning)
rubrics_metrics.description: At a live hearing where cross-examination is permitted/required, parties may not personally question each other; cross-examination must be conducted by an advisor.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a party lacks an advisor, the postsecondary institution must provide one (at no fee or charge) for the purpose of conducting cross-examination. The provided advisor may, but need not be, an attorney. (§106.45(b)(6)(i); discussion at citation 294).

rubrics_metrics.name: Equal opportunity to present witnesses and evidence (§106.45(b)(5)(ii)-(iii))
rubrics_metrics.description: The grievance process must give both parties an equal opportunity to present witnesses (fact and expert) and other inculpatory and exculpatory evidence; recipients may not restrict parties' ability to gather evidence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: 1997 Guidance and later documents reinforce that 'equitable' procedures allow both sides to present witnesses and evidence; the regulations explicitly include these protections.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adequate, reliable, and impartial investigation
rubrics_metrics.description: Investigations must be adequate, reliable, and impartial; ideally carried out by a trained investigator who objectively evaluates credibility, synthesizes all available evidence (both inculpatory and exculpatory), and accounts for unique and complex circumstances of each case.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: 1997 Guidance, 2001 Guidance, and 2017 Q&A emphasize use of trained investigators and objective credibility assessment. Institutions should avoid investigatory bias and ensure reliability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Designated and reasonably prompt timeframes; timeliness standard
rubrics_metrics.description: Grievance procedures should include designated and reasonably prompt timeframes for the major stages of the complaint process; OCR experience notes a typical investigation may take ~60 calendar days though timing varies with complexity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: 1997 and 2001 Guidance recommend prompt timeframes; 2011 Dear Colleague Letter references typical 60-day investigations but recognizes variation depending on complexity and severity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Standard of evidence historically required (preponderance per 2011 guidance)
rubrics_metrics.description: 2011 Dear Colleague Letter indicated that, to be consistent with Title IX standards at that time, schools must use a preponderance-of-the-evidence standard.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The 2011 statement has been influential in guidance history; later documents (2017 Q&A, regulatory changes) discuss evidentiary standards and their application in different eras of guidance/regulation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mediation inappropriate for sexual-assault allegations
rubrics_metrics.description: In some cases — notably alleged sexual assaults — mediation is not appropriate even on a voluntary basis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: 2001 Guidance and the 2011 Dear Colleague Letter explicitly cautioned that mediation should not be used for sexual-assault allegations in many instances.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prohibition on retaliation (§106.71)
rubrics_metrics.description: Regulations expressly prohibit retaliation against any individual exercising rights under Title IX, specifically protecting the right to participate or refuse to participate in a Title IX grievance process.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The final regulations add §106.71 to make anti-retaliation protections explicit; recipients must guard against retaliation in all stages.

rubrics_metrics.name: Emergency removals and administrative leave (§106.44)
rubrics_metrics.description: Respondents may be removed from an education program or activity on an emergency basis; non-student employee respondents may be placed on administrative leave during the pendency of a grievance process; informal resolution may result in agreed sanctions without completing the formal grievance process.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Section 106.44(a)-(d) set out emergency removal and administrative-leave possibilities and the circumstances under which informal resolution may be used to reach an agreement imposing sanctions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clear definitions of roles: complainant and respondent (§106.30)
rubrics_metrics.description: Complainant is defined as an individual alleged to be the victim of conduct that could constitute sexual harassment; respondent is defined as an individual reported to be the perpetrator of such conduct.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Clear statutory/regulatory definitions help structure who may invoke rights and responsibilities under the grievance process and inform notice, investigation, and hearing procedures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Department cannot compel private recipients to violate due process
rubrics_metrics.description: The Department cannot interpret Title IX to require a private recipient to deprive a person of constitutionally-protected due process rights; an agency's regulations must respect constitutional limits on compelling private parties.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analogies to Peterson v. City of Greenville and Truax v. Raich illustrate limits: federal regulatory action cannot force private entities to act in ways that violate constitutional protections.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recipients must adopt and publish prompt and equitable grievance procedures
rubrics_metrics.description: Recipients are required by prior guidance and regulation to adopt and publish grievance procedures that provide for prompt and equitable resolution of sex-discrimination complaints.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: 1997 Guidance, 2001 Guidance, and subsequent documents require published procedures; 'equitable' includes opportunities to present witnesses/evidence and impartial investigation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Trauma-informed approaches should be applied carefully to preserve impartiality
rubrics_metrics.description: Trauma-informed investigation training and approaches can assist in investigations of sexual misconduct but must be applied carefully to ensure that investigations remain impartial.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: White papers (e.g., Betsy DeVos citation summarizing a white paper) caution institutions to balance trauma-informed practices with the need for objectivity and fairness in evidence evaluation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Procedural rights must be provided equally to both parties
rubrics_metrics.description: Any procedural rights (for example, rights concerning cross-examination) must be provided equally to both the complainant and the respondent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: 2017 Q&A stated that procedural rights must be given equally; this equality principle underlies requirements for equal opportunity to present evidence, witnesses, and access to advisors for cross-examination.

rubrics_metrics.name: Regulatory retroactivity limitation for agencies
rubrics_metrics.description: Federal agencies may only create rules with retroactive effect where the authorizing statute expressly grants such authority; retroactivity is disfavored unless required by statutory language.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Administrative Procedure Act references and Bowen v. Georgetown Univ. Hosp. are cited: agencies should not impose regulations retroactively absent clear congressional authorization.

rubrics_metrics.name: Procedural uniformity irrespective of recipient size
rubrics_metrics.description: As a policy matter, the Department does not believe that different Title IX procedures should apply based on the size of a recipient's student body or the recipient's revenues.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Regulatory impact analysis considered small-entity effects but concluded that procedural requirements should be uniform across recipients regardless of size.

rubrics_metrics.name: Criminal-trial protections not required in civil administrative proceedings
rubrics_metrics.description: Protections that apply in criminal trials—such as right to effective assistance of counsel, personal confrontation of witnesses, and proof beyond a reasonable doubt—are not constitutionally required in civil administrative proceedings like Title IX grievance processes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: I.N.S. v. Lopez-Mendoza and other cases are cited to explain the distinction between criminal and civil/admin contexts; institutions should not conflate criminal standards with administrative grievance requirements.
